text: I recently had the pleasure of reviewing a paper on odes and separation of variables. While it was well-written, I noticed some hidden assumptions about boundary conditions that could have used more clarification. Plus, there were a few missing comparisons between different methods that might have strengthened the paper's argument. All in all, though, I appreciate the author taking on such an important and challenging topic!

comments.text: That's great that you caught those assumptions and missing comparisons in the paper. Have you considered what boundary conditions impact sensor accuracy or sensitivity? If so, it might be worth a closer look to ensure they are well-defined and accounted for in the analysis.

text: Closed-loop control feels like cheating until you remember the plant is also cheating by not matching the model.

comments.text: The plant is allowed to be nonlinear, delayed, saturated, and slightly malicious. Your controller is the one with assumptions.
And half those assumptions came from a sensor that was calibrated three months ago.

text: Diff eqs are hard man. They got less annoying once I started asking what I could actually measure instead of trying to symbolically solve everything.

comments.text: Same. For x_dot = Ax, I usually care about the eigenvalues before I care about the exact x(t).
Unless the initial condition lives in a mode you quietly ignored.

text: Property tables are suspiciously good at making materials look memoryless. Creep and hysteresis would like a word.

comments.text: Also strain rate. Two tests at the same temperature can tell very different stories if one takes 30 seconds and the other takes 30 hours.

text: Boundary conditions are where a PDE quietly stops being 'the diffusion equation' and becomes your actual problem.

comments.text: And in the lab, 'T(0)=constant' secretly means 'I own a heater good enough to hold it there.'
Same energy as writing u=0 at a wall and then spending the rest of the day arguing about whether the wall actually behaves that way.

text: Eigenvectors made more sense when I stopped calling them 'special directions' and started thinking: these are directions the transformation only stretches and refuses to rotate.

comments.text: For a real matrix with complex eigenvectors, the transformation would like to file a complaint about that wording.
The geometric version is still useful. It just gets more interesting once the invariant subspace is two-dimensional.

text: I enjoy old papers because they occasionally solve a modern-looking problem using a name nobody searches anymore.

comments.text: The literature search equivalent of changing variables and discovering the integral was tabulated in 1963.

text: A solver giving you six decimal places is not the same thing as the model deserving six decimal places.

comments.text: Numerical precision is very willing to cosplay as physical accuracy.
Especially when the material property you typed in was rounded from a plot in a datasheet.

image_alt: A simple schematic of a cantilever beam fixed at the left wall with a downward point load at the free end. The beam bends downward, and the largest bending moment occurs near the fixed support.
caption: The fixed end is doing a lot of emotional labor here.

comments.text: If this were a strain-gauge setup, I'd put the first gauges near the root before getting fancy anywhere else.
Assuming the root really is fixed. A little compliance there changes the moment distribution more than people like to admit.
